title: Is AI for Contract Review Exciting?
author: Preston Clark · Electra Japonas · Zach Abramowitz

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source presents contract AI as a commercial and democratization opportunity and notes that competitors target major in-house teams, but it does not assess whether corporate legal departments will selectively insource work, become stronger buyers, or reduce particular outside-counsel instructions.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on user capability and workflow redesign rather than model improvement or procurement alone. It materially extends the cluster with a contract-specific account: AI-first tools may absorb legacy CLM functions, but contract data and workflow infrastructure remain necessary, while poorly designed deployment may entrench bespoke drafting and inefficient contracting.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s conditional optimism: it expresses enthusiasm about contract AI while treating adoption as an open trajectory and predicting that legacy business practices may impede organisational change. Its Kodak analogy is speculative rather than evidence of adoption or performance, reinforcing the cluster’s distinction between enthusiasm and proof.
qs: I think a lot will miss the wave, and they'll miss it because sort of the Kodak analogy or whatever, they're just too anchored into their legacy way of doing business, and they just can't, they can't pivot fast enough.
Illuminating as always, and look forward to following the company, and seeing where this adoption goes, obviously, you've convinced me.

st.t: Contract infrastructure: AI challenges siloed CLM systems
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s framing that AI challenges legacy CLM products and architectures without eliminating the underlying need for contract infrastructure. It forecasts AI-review vendors expanding into CLM functions, identifies implementation and scalability problems in incumbent systems, and treats incumbent survival and market signals as unresolved rather than proven.
qs: And if you are a legacy CLM and you happen to not be as good as a LawInsider, or a Harvey, or a Spellbook, you're going to lose because those companies will become CLMs.
But ultimately, if you're a legal team, you need to automate the way you work.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: The source supports the proposition that contract technology should enable and reshape business workflows rather than function only as a repository. It stresses legal-team automation and potentially drastic changes to cross-functional contract processes, while treating the survival of legacy CLM products and branding as uncertain; its replacement claims are forecasts rather than evidence against the underlying need for contract-management functions.

kp.k: Contract AI adoption lags improving capabilities
kp.d: Clark challenges Abramowitz's framing of contract AI as already commoditized: he argues that widespread adoption remains incomplete and estimates saturation is still two or three years away. He reports conversations at a February Miami conference about unsuccessful AI implementations two years earlier, attributing those failures to homegrown systems rather than large language models. These are practitioner observations and forecasts, not measured adoption or performance findings.
qs: So maybe it is boring, but it's still early in the adoption curve.
But I suspect that that's still two or three years away from happening.
They were not using large LLMs like OpenAI and others. And the end result was that it just didn't do what it said it was gonna do.

kp.k: User skills and interfaces determine realized AI value
kp.d: Clark and Japonas argue that useful output depends on users' skills and adoption habits as well as model capabilities. Clark estimates that use of their own product is only one tenth as broad as it should be, stressing repetition, education and interfaces that reveal possible applications. Japonas anticipates lawyer upskilling and creative uses to scale in-house operations or small firms and change business models; these are vendor assessments rather than independently tested results.
qs: I think that that is the curve that requires repetition, it requires education, it requires feature capability awareness
it's still one tenth as broad as it should be.
the functionality and the output of that functionality isn't just dependent on the technology, it's also dependent on the user skill set.

kp.k: AI may require redesigned legal business models
kp.d: Abramowitz suggests existing law-firm business models are an imperfect fit for AI and that the ideal customer may not yet exist. Clark contrasts adding profitable services to an unchanged practice, using cosmetic dentistry as an analogy, with rebuilding the underlying service model. He accepts that AI could challenge firms' financial models, service quality and hourly costs, without presenting evidence of completed restructuring.
qs: the customer that you really want to sell this product to may not even exist yet.
keep your legacy business exactly where it is and how it's functioning. And then just have this little thing on the side that you'll also do that will be super profitable.
it challenges the core of the financial model of how they deliver services, of the quality of the services potentially, of the cost of the services at an hourly rate perspective.

kp.k: Existing distribution supports low-priced contract AI expansion
kp.d: Clark describes bundling a Word add-in and browser AI assistant into LawInsider's existing $29 monthly package to capture market share, while warning that unchanged pricing will not last forever. He reports more than 11,000 customers in more than 50 countries and 50–70 newly activated Word add-in users daily, with approximately 50% coming from existing paying customers during a staggered rollout. His 'democratization' argument concerns wider global access to contracting software, not demonstrated reductions in unmet civil legal need.
qs: pay us $29 a month and you can get access to the law insider database.
we've left it at the same price because we're trying to capture market share. We won't do that forever though.
we have 11,000 plus customers in 50 plus countries who use us, pay us, and are very happy.
LawInsider is now adding between 50 and 70 new activated users every day, into the word add-in who are using it.
So right now, it's at about 50%, but that is a byproduct of us staggering the rollout

kp.k: Standards create network effects absent from clause libraries
kp.d: Clark says LawInsider's clause-copying business lacked referrals and team expansion despite substantial usage. Japonas describes 1NDA's alternative mechanism: prominent corporate adopters encouraged their law firms to participate, while sending the standard agreement exposed counterparties to an adoption link. She reports around 6,000 organic adopters over three years. The acquisition combines LawInsider's distribution with this community-supported standardization model.
qs: there's no network effects, there's no team player model.
I asked them to go and ask their law firms to also come in to the project.
Because every time someone sends one NDA to the other side, the other side may not have seen it. Now they have. There's a link on it. They can go and adopt it.
over the course of three years, we amassed around 6,000 adopters.

kp.k: Unconstrained AI could worsen contracting complexity
kp.d: Japonas warns that generating bespoke NDAs with ChatGPT could undermine standardization rather than solve contracting waste. She uses word processing and email as a historical analogy, asserting that easier copying and redlining expanded contracts from 10 to 100 pages. Abramowitz extends the concern to AI-readable agreements becoming excessively long; Japonas raises a further concern about meaningful agreement when AI does everything. These are arguments and possible downstream outcomes, not documented AI effects or legal findings.
qs: people will see that as a better solution to just go on creating more bespoke language, which is the absolute last thing this industry needs.
when we invented word processing, all of a sudden contracts went from 10 pages to 100 because it's much easier to copy and paste
Where's the meeting of the minds that contracts are meant to be? Without a meeting of the minds, there is no real contract. If AI is just doing it all, then there is none.

kp.k: Codified playbooks extend standards to third-party contracts
kp.d: Japonas proposes translating 1NDA's explicit and implicit rules into an AI playbook for reviewing counterparties' NDAs. She presents this as a pragmatic interim mechanism while standard-template adoption remains incomplete: users can uphold the standard's intended fairness and balance without requiring every counterparty to adopt the template. More broadly, she argues that review rules, rather than AI alone, determine value.
qs: 1NDA is a static template, but it's also a set of rules, some of which are explicitly stated in the document and some of which are not.
we can create an AI playbook that people can use to review third-party NDAs and still uphold the standard.
we're being pragmatic because 1NDA has not been adopted by a million organizations yet.
the rules against which AI is going to review a contract ultimately is the thing that's going to give you the value

kp.k: Contract databases become inputs for review and comparison
kp.d: Japonas claims LawInsider's accumulated contract data and clause-usage information enable automated, data-driven playbook creation and comparisons of generated clauses with market practice. Clark describes a clause-level LawInsider index score and links to similarly drafted or more standard clauses, intended to expose unusual counterparty provisions. These are vendor descriptions of product functionality and differentiation; the transcript supplies no independent accuracy testing or evidence that frequency establishes legal quality.
qs: LawInsider allows us to build these playbooks at scale, because we have the data and we have the automation to create these playbooks that are very data driven.
we can tell you how much usage there's been of a certain clause drafted in a certain way
you can benchmark a third-party contract clause by clause and get a LawInsider index score alongside each clause
We want to find as many ways as we can to inject the value of the database that we have that we've built up over the years into the tool.

kp.k: Early adoption can build cumulative organizational advantages
kp.d: Abramowitz argues against treating waiting for second-wave products as costless. Drawing on his observations of firms that began technology adoption in 2017, he suggests learning and participation can yield cumulative benefits even when initial products change. He qualifies the argument by warning against becoming attached to a particular early technology; no comparative firm-performance data are supplied.
qs: it's firms that started this like in 2017, right?
There is compounding interest to early adoption if you play it right. You can't get so tied to what it is you early adopt.

kp.k: Contract certification offers another route to faster agreement
kp.d: Clark praises Term Scout's Certify concept as a way for businesses to publish contracts and demonstrate their balance to accelerate signature. He explicitly labels his suggestion that Certify received less attention than AI as speculation without inside information. The discussion treats certification, standard forms and AI review as overlapping approaches to contracting problems rather than identical products. Abramowitz discloses his involvement in the Screens transaction and continuing Agiloft stockholding.
qs: the idea that Stripe would publish one of its contracts for the benefit of its users to get to Signature faster
demonstrate the balanced nature of something. It's a wonderful thesis.
I'm just speculating because I don't have any insider information on this
I suspect it didn't get the oxygen that AI did.
I'm just a holder of Agiloft stock now.

kp.k: AI review could become the entry point for CLM
kp.d: Clark argues that storing in-house contract data and automating routine workflows remain valuable, but claims legacy contract lifecycle management vendors are not doing AI review well. He predicts AI review will become the entry point to broader contract management and that providers such as Spellbook and Harvey will add CLM capabilities, potentially without that label. These are competitive assessments and forecasts, not established product roadmaps.
qs: It's really valuable to store in-house contract data. It's really valuable to own the workflow automation for routine contracts within an in-house team.
I know that there's no CLM, legacy CLM in this caliber that you just said, that is crushing AI review.
I think that this is the entry point for CLM.
You don't think Spellbook is going to become a CLM. Of course they are.
they're going to become a full CLM.

kp.k: Funding shifts underpin host's forecast of CLM disruption
kp.d: Abramowitz interprets an unpublished slide using CB Insights data as evidence of declining CLM funding relative to legal AI agents and copilots, while acknowledging imperfect category definitions and that funding is not determinative. The transcript provides no figures from the slide. He predicts difficulties for legacy vendors and possible reinvention of organizational contracting workflows, and interprets Agiloft's Screens acquisition as a response to that challenge.
qs: this is CB Insights data.
I don't think that their definition of legal AI agents and co-pilots is perfect.
I'm not trying to say that everything follows the funding
the life cycle of a contract inside of an organization might change drastically.
I think that's why they bought screens, because they said, we're going to have to completely rebuild our product around screens.

kp.k: Legal workflow automation remains necessary despite CLM difficulties
kp.d: Japonas counters the strongest claims of CLM obsolescence, describing it as an operating system supporting a legal team's working model. Drawing on her implementation consulting experience, she attributes difficulties to diverse departmental priorities and a tension between customization and scalable software. She argues that back-office automation will remain necessary, although it may be renamed or unbundled into standalone tools that deliver value faster.
qs: I think CLM is necessary.
It's an operating system for your legal team.
every in-house legal team needs a malleability that is at odds with a scalable tech product.
the need to automate your back office as a legal team will always be required.
whether we unbundle CLM and we go ahead and we offer just standalone tools that get you to value quicker, is a different topic.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Clark argues that AI contracting capabilities are diffusing quickly, but widespread adoption remains incomplete.
pts.d: Preston Clark distinguishes rapidly converging vendor capabilities from actual adoption by lawyers. He predicts that saturation in AI drafting and review is still two or three years away. Electra Japonas adds that effective capability depends on user skill as well as technology: creative use could scale internal legal operations and small firms or change their business models.

pts.k: Clark presents AI as potentially disruptive to the core economics of legal services, rather than merely a supplementary offering.
pts.d: Clark tentatively agrees that legacy business models may need to be rebuilt because AI challenges service delivery, quality and hourly costs. He contrasts this with adding a profitable new service while leaving the existing business untouched; he does not provide a quantified prediction of savings or revenue effects.

pts.k: Japonas warns that unconstrained AI drafting could perpetuate bespoke-contract proliferation; standards-based AI review offers a different approach.
pts.d: Japonas argues that generating more bespoke NDAs with ChatGPT could undermine 1NDA's effort to reduce repetitive contracting work. She proposes codifying the template's explicit and implicit rules into AI playbooks so that adopters can review counterparties' documents against the standard. Her concern about AI doing everything and eroding a meeting of minds is a prospective argument, not a reported legal finding.

pts.k: Japonas and Clark claim that contract data and playbooks make AI review more useful by supplying rules and clause-level comparisons.
pts.d: Japonas identifies the rules used for review, rather than AI alone, as the source of value. She says LawInsider's accumulated contract and usage data support automated playbook creation and comparison of generated clauses. Clark describes clause-level index scores and access to more standard examples. These are product-capability claims; the transcript provides no independent accuracy test. The benchmarking described here concerns contract clauses, not model performance on a test set.

pts.k: Clark predicts that AI review vendors will expand into contract lifecycle management, while Japonas maintains that legal workflow automation remains necessary.
pts.d: Clark calls AI review an entry point into CLM and predicts that Harvey and Spellbook will add full CLM capabilities, potentially without adopting that label. He expects legacy providers with inferior AI review to lose ground. Japonas distinguishes the continuing need to automate legal-team operations from the CLM label or bundled product form, allowing for standalone tools that deliver value faster.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Clark supports the distribution-led adoption thesis with LawInsider's self-reported activation and customer figures.
pts.d: Clark reports 50–70 newly activated Word add-in users daily, an existing customer base exceeding 11,000 across more than 50 countries, and approximately half of current activations coming from existing paying customers. He also reports 5,000–10,000 new free accounts monthly. These figures support his account of uptake through established distribution, not independently measured legal quality, productivity or market-wide adoption.

pts.k: Claims about adoption barriers and contracting outcomes draw on customer anecdotes, product observations, historical analogy and consulting experience.
pts.d: Clark cites discussions with large-firm users about unsuccessful earlier AI implementations and says existing customers use only a fraction of his product's possible applications. Japonas cites roughly 6,000 organically acquired 1NDA adopters over three years as evidence for standards' network effects, not AI adoption. Her claim that technology can worsen contracting uses word processing as an analogy. Her explanation of CLM implementation difficulties draws on her own consulting experience. No controlled outcome study or independent comparative benchmark is supplied for these claims or the vendor-convergence predictions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Broad adoption is forecast over a two-to-three-year horizon, conditional on learning and usable product design.
pts.d: At the time of the 2025 episode, Clark places AI contracting saturation approximately two or three years ahead. He describes improvement in adoption and quality over a two-to-three-year horizon, while stressing repetition, education, awareness and interfaces that surface use cases. Japonas similarly conditions transformation on lawyers developing skills and imagining applications. These are qualified expectations, not firm implementation deadlines.

pts.k: Standards-based review is an interim strategy; low-price bundling and the existing-customer activation mix are explicitly temporary.
pts.d: Japonas expects standards adoption to snowball only after sufficient uptake and positions third-party NDA review as pragmatic while universal template adoption remains distant. Clark says the AI bundle retains the legacy price to capture market share but will not do so forever. He expects activations eventually to shift toward approximately 90% new users as promotion to the installed base is completed. He gives no dates for these transitions.

pts.k: Legacy software displacement depends on incumbents' ability to adapt; no deadline is given for AI vendors becoming CLMs.
pts.d: Clark qualifies the disruption thesis by allowing that sufficiently fast-moving enterprise SaaS companies can respond successfully. He predicts that others will miss the transition because of attachment to legacy practices. His specific predictions about Harvey and Spellbook entering CLM have no stated completion date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Lawyers, small firms and in-house teams face skill changes and potential scaling opportunities; LawInsider targets its existing international customer base.
pts.d: Japonas anticipates upskilling and creative application by lawyers, including scaling small practices and internal legal operations. She also stresses ease of use because busy lawyers resist learning complicated interfaces. Clark frames bundling AI into LawInsider's existing subscription as wider distribution of capabilities through its international customer base. This democratization claim concerns access to professional software; the source does not demonstrate reduced unmet civil legal need.

pts.k: Contracting counterparties, standards adopters, in-house buyers and competing software vendors are affected differently.
pts.d: Japonas intends standards-based AI to help organizational adopters preserve balanced NDA terms when counterparties supply their own documents. In-house teams continue to need workflow automation tailored to differing priorities. On the provider side, Clark predicts competition between legacy CLM vendors and AI software companies expanding into their functions; these are legal-tech vendors rather than alternative legal service providers delivering legal work.
